UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                  BEFORE THE
                    FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                    )
    Southern Indiana Gas and Electric Company       )
    v. Midcontinent Independent System              )          Docket No. EL26-38-001
    Operator, Inc.                                  )
                                                    )


REQUEST FOR REHEARING OF THE SIERRA CLUB, ENVIRONMENTAL LAW &
  POLICY CENTER, CITIZENS ACTION COALITION OF INDIANA, CITIZENS
UTILITY BOARD OF WISCONSIN, CITIZENS UTILITY BOARD OF ILLINOIS, AND
                         PUBLIC CITIZEN


         Pursuant to Section 313(a) of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) and Rule 713 of the Rules

of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or

“FERC”),1 Sierra Club, the Environmental Law & Policy Center, Citizens Action Coalition of

Indiana, Citizens Utility Board of Wisconsin, Citizens Utility Board of Illinois, and Public

Citizen (collectively “Public Interest Organizations” or “PIOs”) respectfully submit this request

for rehearing of the Commission’s March 19, 2026 Order (“Order”) in the above-captioned

proceeding, granting Southern Indiana Gas and Electric Company’s (“SIGE”) complaint against

the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (“MISO”).2

I.       Introduction

         SIGE brought its complaint in response to the Department of Energy (“DOE” or “the

Department”) order issued December 23, 2025 directing Unit 2 of the F.B. Culley generating

plant (“Culley”) to operate past its planned retirement date (“December DOE Order”).3 The DOE

  S. Ind. Gas and Electric Co. v. Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc, 194 FERC ¶ 61,214.

  Department of Energy Order No. 202-25-13 (Dec. 23, 2025). The DOE has since issued a second order

(hereinafter “March DOE Order”) (collectively “DOE Orders”).


                                                   1
 Order was issued pursuant to Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”), but did not

comply with the requirements the FPA mandates for such orders, and improperly disregarded the

resource adequacy efforts and findings of state authorities, MISO, and this Commission, which

together had already ensured that MISO North and Central regions have sufficient capacity.4

Numerous parties, including many of the PIOs, have challenged the December DOE Order in the

United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit.5 As PIOs explained in their

initial protest (“PIOs Protest”), the Commission’s Order exacerbates the Department’s mistakes

and further violates the FPA by approving cost recovery for the Culley in a manner that does not

ensure costs will be allocated commensurate with benefits.6 PIOs request that the Commission

grant rehearing to 1) explain what benefits Culley provides that remain uncompensated under the

current tariff; 2) revisit the Commission’s treatment of Culley as a capacity resource despite clear

language in the DOE Orders prohibiting such consideration; and 3) explain how demand-based

load ratio share properly matches costs to benefits.

II.       Request for Rehearing

           A.     Statement of Issues

      1. The Order is arbitrary and capricious, unsupported by substantial evidence, and not the
         product of reasoned decision-making because it failed to respond to substantial questions
         raised by PIOs in the proceeding. 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A); Bloomberg L.P. v. SEC, 45 F.4th
         462, 476−77 (D.C. Cir. 2022) (“[A]n agency’s response to public comments must be
         sufficient to enable the courts to see what major issues of policy were ventilated and why
         the agency reacted to them as it did.”) (cleaned up).
      2. The Order exceeds the Commission’s jurisdiction and statutory authority by violating
         FPA Section 202(c)’s requirement that rates be just and reasonable, which encompasses
         the principle that utilities that pay for a facility must benefit from that facility’s operation.
         16 U.S.C §§ 824a, 824d(a); Illinois Com. Comm’n v. FERC, 576 F.3d 470, 476 (7th Cir.

4

Environmental Council, Environmental Law and Policy Center, and Public Citizen, Motion to Intervene
and Request for Rehearing and Stay of DOE Order No. 202-25-13 (Jan 22, 2026), available at
https://www.energy.gov/ceser/federal-power-act-section-202c-culley-order-no-202-25-13.
5
  Petition for Review, Sierra Club v. DOE, Case No. 26-1057 (D.C. Cir. 2026).
6
  PIOs Protest, Docket No. EL26-38-000, Accession No. 20260126-5297 (Jan. 26, 2026).


                                                     2
          2009) (“FERC is not authorized to approve a pricing scheme that requires a group of
         utilities to pay for facilities from which its members derive no benefits, or benefits that
         are trivial in relation to the costs sought to be shifted to its members.”); K N Energy, Inc.
         v. FERC, 968 F.2d 1295, 1300 (D.C. Cir. 1992) (“[I]t has been traditionally required that
         all approved rates reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer who
         must pay them.”).
      3. The Order is arbitrary and capricious, unsupported by substantial evidence, and not the
         product of reasoned decision making for reaching a conclusion regarding the
         beneficiaries of Culley’s continued operation that has no rational basis in the record. 5
         U.S.C. § 706(2)(A); 16 U.S.C. § 825l(b). See also, Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n of U.S.,
         Inc. v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983); PPL Wallingford Energy
         LLC v. FERC, 419 F.3d 1194, 1198 (D.C. Cir. 2005); FPL Energy Maine Hydro LLC v.
         FERC, 287 F.3d 1151 (D.C. Cir. 2002); California Pub. Utils. Comm’n v. FERC, 20
         F.4th 795, 802 (D.C. Cir. 2021); Delaware Div. of Pub. Advoc. v. FERC, 3 F.4th 461, 469
         (D.C. Cir. 2021).
      4. The Order is arbitrary and capricious, unsupported by substantial evidence, and contrary
         to law under Section 202, 16 U.S.C § 824d(a), for seemingly relying on the Department’s
         unlawful emergency declaration as the sole basis for the conclusion that an emergency
         exists in the MISO North and Central zones and that there is a shortage of capacity in
         these zones, in spite of clear evidence to the contrary. 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A).

          B.     Argument in Support of Rehearing

                 1.      The Commission does not justify its reading of the DOE Orders to allow
                         consideration of Culley as a capacity resource.

          The DOE Orders are clear: Culley “shall not be considered a capacity resource.”7 As

PIOs explained, the most straightforward reading that respects this requirement would prohibit

the Commission from treating the unit as a capacity resource.8 And without the ability to

recognize a capacity benefit from the units, it is not just and reasonable for the Commission to

assign costs associated with Culley’s capacity value to any MISO participants. The

Commission’s response to PIOs’ citation of the December DOE Order was to ascribe an entirely

different directive to the December DOE Order: that Culley cannot be counted as capacity

resources in the MISO resource adequacy construct, but is to be considered capacity resources in



7
    December DOE Order at 6; March DOE Order at 9.
8
    PIOs Protest at 10−11.



                                                   3
 every other respect.9 But the Commission’s sole justification for its reading, which goes against

the plain language of the December DOE Order, is that the December DOE Order cited resource

adequacy concerns as the justification for the order. DOE’s stated overarching basis for its order,

however, is no reason to ignore the plain language of its directive: Culley “shall not be

considered a capacity resource.”10 The Commission must either provide a valid justification for

its strained interpretation of the actual language of the DOE Orders, or it must state why it does

not believe the DOE Orders’ discussion of capacity role for Culley is binding.11

                2. The Commission has not explained why over-procurement of capacity
                   provides a benefit to ratepayers or what benefits remain uncompensated
                   under the current tariff.

        Even putting aside the clear language of the DOE Orders, PIOs provided evidence that

the Culley did not provide a capacity benefit to MISO customers because each zone in MISO had

already met its capacity obligation.12 The Commission did not address this argument in its Order,

instead stating that DOE “indicat[es] that resource adequacy concerns for [zones 1−7] were the

driver for the DOE Order.”13 But the Commission has also previously recognized that over-

procuring capacity can lead to unjust and unreasonable rates,14 and that the amount of capacity

MISO requires customers to source under its resource adequacy construct is just and

11
   FCC v. Prometheus Radio Project, 592 U.S. 414, 423 (2021) (“The [Administrative Procedure Act]’s
arbitrary-and-capricious standard requires that agency action be reasonable and reasonably explained.”).
12
   PIOs Protest at 10−11 and n.39.
13
   Order at P 35.
14
   See, e.g., New York Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 179 FERC ¶ 61,102 at P 39 (2022) (accepting a tariff
revision because it reduced the risk of “at least three significant harms” including “over-procurement of
capacity”); ISO New Eng. Inc., 165 FERC ¶ 61,202 at P 83 (2018) (discussing cases in which the
Commission rejected tariff revisions because “it would require ratepayers to pay twice for the same
capacity need and would result in over-procuring capacity”).



                                                    4
 reasonable.15 The Commission’s Order here undermines those previous findings by forcing

customers to pay for capacity greater than that required by the MISO resource adequacy

construct, without offering any reasoning for its departure from previous Commission orders.

The Commission must explain itself to the extent it departs from its previous reasoning in order

to meet its obligations under the Administrative Procedure Act.16

        The Commission also failed to adequately respond to PIOs’ argument that current tariff

provisions fully compensate Culley for any cognizable benefits it may provide MISO

customers.17 The Order states that “[w]hile existing Tariff provisions govern the distribution of

market revenues for any energy supplied by Market Participants, they do not provide a cost

allocation method for prudently incurred costs associated with orders issued under FPA section

202(c).”18 But that statement is nonresponsive to the argument in PIOs Protest, which focuses on

compensation for actual benefits provided. Neither the Commission in its Order nor SIGE in its

protest have explained what benefits Culley provides that are not already compensated through

existing tariff mechanisms. It is unjust and unreasonable for customers to be allocated costs that

are not associated with commensurate benefits.19 The fact that the current tariff does not permit

adequacy construct).

   FCC v. Fox TV Stations, Inc., 556 U.S. 502, 515 (2009) (agencies must provide reasoned explanation
for departing from prior policies).

made, demanded, or received by any public utility for or in connection with the transmission or sale of
electric energy be just and reasonable. For decades, the FERC and the courts have understood this
requirement to incorporate a cost-causation principle.”) (cleaned up); Long Island Power Auth. & Long
Island Lighting Co. v. FERC, 27 F.4th 705, 709 (D.C. Cir. 2022)) (“To be just and reasonable, rates must
‘reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer who must pay for them.’ This ‘cost-
causation principle’ requires ‘comparing the costs assessed against a party to the burdens imposed or



                                                   5
 recovery of 202(c) order compliance costs is irrelevant if the tariff already provides adequate

compensation for all of the benefits Culley provides.

        In fact, Culley is not providing capacity benefits as understood in the context of MISO.

Capacity obligations provide an important planning value, for reliability.20 But if Culley is

unable to participate in MISO’s capacity construct, then it is not clear what capacity planning

value Culley can provide. And, as PIOs have previously discussed, the units’ real-time reliability

contribution is already compensated through Value of Lost Load (“VOLL”) pricing.21 As such,

it remains entirely unclear what uncompensated benefits Culley is providing.

    3. The Commission has not explained how demand-based load ratio share properly
       allocates costs according to benefits.

        PIOs Protest explained that a just cost-allocation mechanism must identify benefits, and

then match benefits to beneficiaries.22 The Commission’s response to PIOs’ arguments fails to

resolve significant questions as to how demand-based load ratio share will accurately allocate

costs according to benefits. PIOs recognize that this proceeding does not determine what, if any,

costs can be recovered. But the tariff language and cost allocation decisions the Commission

makes in this proceeding will provide guideposts for more fact-specific inquiries down the line,

which will help determine the justness and reasonableness of the specific costs and cost

allocation that are determined in those later proceedings. Clear Commission findings identifying




benefits drawn by that party.’” (citing Midwest ISO Transmission Owners v. FERC, 373 F.3d 1361, 1368
(D.C. Cir. 2004)) (cleaned up).
20
   Coalition of MISO Transmission Customers v. Midcontinent Indep. Sys., 181 FERC ¶ 61,005 at P 63
(2022) (“MISO's capacity construct is designed to not only place capacity requirements on LSEs to
promote resource adequacy in a given Planning Year, but also to produce price signals that promote long-
term resource adequacy and economic efficiency.”).
21
   PIOs Protest at 11−12.
22
   Id. at 13−14.



                                                   6
 what benefits the units might provide, and who those benefits might accrue to, is critical to

ensure actual costs are ultimately allocated commensurate with benefits.

       As noted in PIOs Protest, the relative benefit each of MISO zones 1−7 will receive from

the delayed retirement of Culley remains unclear, as does the reasonableness of allocating costs

among zones 1−7 using a demand-based load ratio share methodology.23 The Order does not

provide a reasoned response to this argument. While the Commission stated that it found a load-

ratio-share methodology based on peak demand to be justified in a parallel proceeding regarding

cost allocation for the Campbell plant while it operates pursuant to a 202(c) order,24 the

Campbell order did not explain why load ratio share properly allocated costs amongst the zones.

Instead, the Campbell order provided reasoning why costs should be allocated on a demand,

rather than energy, basis, and summarily stated that “forecasted Season coincident peak demand

for Local Resource Zones 1-7 for the duration of the DOE Order (and any extensions) …

reasonably aligns with the emergency described in the DOE Order and the beneficiaries of the

emergency energy provided by the Campbell Plant.”25 This cursory statement lacks sufficient

reasoning to meet the APA’s requirement that the Commission explains its reasoning in this

docket.26

       It is also not clear why the Commission’s conclusion in the Campbell proceeding should

apply in this proceeding. In the Campbell proceeding, the Commission agreed with intervenor

Consumer Alliance that the costs associated the Campbell plant’s 202(c) order should be



23
   Id.
24
   Order at P 36.
25
   Consumers Energy Co. v. Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 192 FERC ¶ 61,158 at P 43 (2025).
26
   Encino Motorcars, LLC v. Navarro, 579 U.S. 211, 221 (2016) (an agency’s explanation must be “clear
enough that its ‘path may reasonably be discerned.’” (quoting Bowman Transp., Inc. v. Arkansas-Best
Freight System, Inc., 419 U.S. 281, 286 (1974))).



                                                  7
 allocated on a demand basis “because the costs relate to capacity.”27 But in the case of the

Campbell plant, the relevant 202(c) order was silent regarding whether the Campbell plant could

be considered a capacity resource. Here, by contrast, the DOE Orders prohibit considering

Culley as a capacity resource, which as explained above dramatically reframes the benefits

Culley can realistically provide to the MISO system.

        Moreover, the record in this proceeding contains no evidence that benefits from Culley

will accrue roughly proportionate to zonal peak demand. Each zone has different amounts of

uncleared capacity and a different level of reliance on capacity imports from other zones.28 Even

if zones 1−7 were short on capacity and Culley was required to supplement existing generation

capacity on the system, zones with larger quantities of excess capacity would presumably need

less of the capacity from Culley than zones with less excess capacity. Thus, even then the

benefits would not track with zonal peak demand but rather would be inversely proportional to

uncleared capacity. Furthermore, to the extent that the plants are needed to meet future demand,

allocating costs using current zonal demand is unjustified as it is the future peak load

contributions and available resource levels that will dictate future capacity needs.29

        Finally, even putting aside the fact that Culley is not authorized to provide capacity

services, allocating all costs on a demand basis still may not be justified because it does not

capture all of Culley’s benefit streams. PIOs noted that Culley is providing energy benefits by

   MISO, Planning Resource Auction Results for Planning Year 2025-26, at 18-21 (May, 29, 2025)

   The DOE orders suggest that at least part of the need it purports to identify is future need. See March
DOE Order at 5 (“The evidence indicates that there is also a potential longer-term resource adequacy

                                                    8
 virtue of its participation in MISO-run energy markets.30 Any revenue from Culley’s

participation in the energy and ancillary services markets untethers the ultimate cost of the units

from any resource adequacy benefit they may be providing, making it even less tenable to

allocate costs based on a demand rather than energy basis.

        In making these arguments, PIOs are not trying to pre-judge the prudence of any incurred

costs. Rather, these concerns point to situations in which the rigid cost allocation mechanism that

SIGE proposed and the Commission approved will result in an unjust and unreasonable

allocation of costs that might otherwise be prudent. Because the Commission has failed to

identify the benefits Culley provides, these conflicts are all but inevitable. It is also why, as

discussed in PIOs’ Protest, a hearing is warranted.31

III.    Conclusion

        For the reasons given above, PIOs respectfully request that the Commission grant

rehearing to revisit the proposed recovery for Culley and to provide updated guidance on how to

calculate the beneficiaries of Culley’s delayed retirement.




Respectfully submitted,                                                 Dated: April 20, 2026
